title: On watchful guard
core: All four describe a guard that hasn't been lowered — attention held because something might go wrong. They split on four axes: what the watching is pointed at (a specific party, a general threat, your own next move, nothing in particular), whether it's sustained or a reflex, whether it stops you acting, and whether the speaker admires you for it or is quietly mocking you. Two are compliments, one is neutral, one is a put-down.
exam_note: Sentence equivalence loves pairing **wary** with **circumspect** — check whether the caution is pointed outward at a suspect thing or inward at your own next move; and check the sentence's tone, since **skittish** sneers where **vigilant** praises.

words.nuance: The only one with a named object — you are wary **of** someone, of an offer, of a clause in the contract. It's distrust of a particular party, and it doesn't stop you: you sign the deal, wary, watching his hands.

Not a reaction to any one suspect but a **post you hold** — sustained indefinitely, scanning for threat that may never come. It's the only member that's outright praise, and the only one that describes a duty rather than a feeling: sentries, auditors, night nurses.

The watching is aimed at **your own conduct**, not at an external threat — you survey the consequences and hold your tongue or your signature. Alone in the group it brakes action, and alone in the group it's formal: a diplomat is circumspect, a horse never is.

The only involuntary one — a hair trigger, not a judgement, and the reaction is **out of proportion** to what caused it. Calling investors skittish says they're flinching rather than reasoning; the word belittles, and it drags along a whiff of the barnyard it came from.
